lesson.intro: Interviews mix in a second tier of structures that each solve one kind of problem far better than anything else: tries for prefixes, union-find for groups, prefix sums for ranges, monotonic stacks for "next larger", grid walks, and designs such as an LRU cache.
objectives: Implement a trie for prefix lookups, autocomplete, wildcards and grid word search
Build union-find with path compression and union by rank, and apply it to groups, cycles and trees
Answer range and subarray questions with prefix sums, difference arrays and a running total plus a map
Apply monotonic stacks and the standard grid patterns to new problems
Design an O(1) LRU cache from a hash map and a doubly linked list

sections.title: Tries: words stored by their prefixes
sections.key: A trie stores words along shared prefix paths, so insert, search and prefix checks each cost O(L) for a word of length L, however many words it holds.
sections.body:
Type `car` into a search box with 100,000 product names behind it. A hash set can tell you whether `card` is a word in O(L), but not which words start with `car` without checking every one.

A **trie** (prefix tree, said "try") answers that. Each node is a prefix: the root is the empty prefix, each edge adds one letter, and each node holds a map from letter to child plus an **end flag** where a complete word stops. Words that begin the same way share a path.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

The price is memory: every node carries its own map, so a trie often takes several times the memory of a set holding the same words.

[[visual 3]]

[[code]]

visual.title: car, card, care, cat
visual.caption: Green nodes have the end flag set. All four words share the c and a nodes.

visual.title: Three operations, each O(L)
rows: Walk the letters, creating missing children, then set the end flag on the last node
Walk the letters. True only if the walk succeeds **and** the last node's end flag is set
Walk the letters. True if the walk succeeds at all

items.title: Trie
points: Lists every word that starts with a prefix
Checks whether any word starts with a prefix
Longest common prefix, autocomplete, spell check, word games
Routers use tries for longest prefix match
Several times the memory of a set

items.title: Hash set
points: Exact lookup: is `card` stored? O(L)
Prefix questions mean scanning every word
Compact

sections.deeper:
**Storing children.** A dict works for any alphabet and stays compact when most letters are missing. A fixed array of 26 slots indexes faster but only fits lowercase letters and wastes space when most slots are empty.

**Routing tables.** A router must find the longest prefix in its table that matches a destination address. Many implementations keep the forwarding table in a trie over the address bits, so the lookup walks one bit at a time and remembers the last node that held a route.
sections.tip: When you will report whole words later (autocomplete, grid search), store the word itself at its end node instead of a True flag, so you never rebuild strings from the path.
sections.pitfall: Forgetting the end flag. Without it, search("car") returns True after inserting only "card", because the path c, a, r exists. search needs the walk and the flag; startsWith only the walk.

activity.title: Count the nodes each word creates
activity.prompt: Run it and connect each number to the diagram: "ten" reuses the t and e nodes, so it adds only one. Then do the task and predict both new numbers before you run it.

props.task: Change the list to ["tea", "ten", "to", "team", "tea"]. How many nodes do "team" and the second "tea" create?
props.expectOutput:
tea: created 3
ten: created 1
to: created 1
team: created 1
tea: created 0

check.question: A trie holds only "card" and "care". What do search("car") and startsWith("car") return?
choices: True and True
False and True
False and False
True and False
check.explanation: The walk c, a, r succeeds, so startsWith is True. No word ends at the r node, so its end flag is off and search is False. Inserting "car" itself would flip search to True.

sections.title: Searching below a node: autocomplete, wildcards and word grids
sections.key: The subtree below a prefix's node holds every completion of that prefix, so autocomplete, wildcard matching and grid word search are walks plus a depth-first search.
sections.body:
Once you can walk to a prefix's node, everything below it completes that prefix. Two classic problems build on that:

[[visual]]

**Many words in one grid.** Searching a letter grid separately for each of thousands of words repeats the same walks for words that share prefixes. Put the words in a trie instead, and run one search from each cell carrying the current trie node:

[[visual 2]]

A path dies the moment it stops being a prefix of any word.

For a fixed word list, mention the simple alternative: sort the words, binary search for the first word that is at least the prefix, and read forward while words still match. It uses far less memory, at O(L log n) per query instead of an O(L) walk.

[[code]]

visual.title: Below the prefix node
rows: Walk to the prefix node (O(P)), then depth-first search below it, visiting children in sorted letter order: words come out alphabetically. Stop once you have k
Insert the words in **sorted order** and let each node keep the first three words that pass through it: those are its three smallest completions. Each keystroke is one step and an O(1) read
Letters walk normally; a `.` branches into every child. At the end of the pattern, succeed only on a node with its end flag set, which also enforces the length

steps.label: Insert every word into a trie
Start a depth-first search from each grid cell with the trie root
Step to a neighbor only if the trie node has a child for its letter
steps.detail: Mark the cell as used on this path

steps.label: Reach a word's end node: record it, then clear that mark
steps.detail: So a word traced along two paths is reported once

steps.label: Restore the cell when backtracking out of it

sections.deeper:
**Cost of a wildcard.** Each dot can multiply the branches by the alphabet size, but the trie prunes every branch that no stored word follows, so real searches stay small.

**Cost of autocomplete.** The walk costs O(P) for a prefix of length P, and collecting costs the size of the subtree below it. That is why you stop at k suggestions, or precompute the top three per node when one trie serves many keystrokes.
sections.pitfall: Reporting the same word twice in the grid search because it can be traced along two different paths. Remove the word's end mark as soon as you record it.

activity.title: Autocomplete suggestions
activity.prompt: Insert the words in sorted order and let each node keep up to three of them, then walk the typed letters. Test a prefix that matches nothing before you submit: every later entry must be empty too.

check.question: Why is one trie-guided search faster than running a separate grid search for each of thousands of words?
choices: A trie stores the grid cells, so neighbors are found in O(1)
A trie sorts the words, so the grid can be binary searched
Words with a common prefix share one walk through the grid, and a path stops as soon as it is no word's prefix
A trie lets each cell be reused within a word, so fewer paths are needed
check.explanation: Shared prefixes are explored once, and the trie prunes dead paths immediately. The trie holds the words, not the grid, and cells still cannot be reused within one word.

sections.title: Union-find: path compression and union by rank
sections.key: Union-find stores each group as a tree whose root names it; with union by rank and path compression, find and union run in effectively constant time.
sections.body:
Friendships arrive one at a time, and between arrivals you must answer "are Ana and Raj in the same group?" A fresh BFS each time costs O(V + E). **Union-find** (disjoint set union, DSU) answers in nearly constant time.

It keeps one array, `parent`. A **root** points to itself and names its group.

- **find(x)**: follow parents from x up to the root. Same root, same group.
- **union(a, b)**: find both roots; if they differ, make one the parent of the other.

Naive unions can build a long chain, so one find costs O(n). Two tricks fix that:

[[visual]]

With both, m operations cost O(m α(n)). α, the inverse Ackermann function, is at most 4 for any real input, so treat each operation as constant time.

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

[[code]]

items.title: Union by rank
points: Each root keeps a **rank**, an upper bound on its tree's height
Hang the lower-rank root under the higher one
Only equal ranks raise the survivor's rank by 1
Height stays O(log n); union by size works as well

items.title: Path compression
points: While find walks up, point every node it passes straight at the root
Recursive: `parent[x] = find(parent[x])`
Path halving does the same in a loop

visual.title: One find(7) with path compression
visual.caption: 7 and 6 now point straight at the root 0. After compression, ranks are upper bounds, not exact heights.

sections.tip: In Python, a recursive find on a very long chain can hit the recursion limit before compression flattens it. Union by rank keeps trees O(log n) tall, or use the loop version with path halving.
sections.pitfall: Linking the items instead of their roots: `parent[b] = a` instead of `parent[find(b)] = find(a)`. It pulls b out of its old group and leaves the rest of that group behind.

activity.title: Watch ranks decide the root
activity.prompt: Run it and check the parent array against the unions: 0 and 2 both had rank 1, so 2 went under 0 and 0's rank became 2. Then do the task.

props.code:
parent = list(range(6))
rank = [0] * 6

def find(x):
    if parent[x] != x:
        parent[x] = find(parent[x])     # path compression
    return parent[x]

def union(a, b):
    ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
    if ra == rb:
        return False
    if rank[ra] < rank[rb]:
        ra, rb = rb, ra
    parent[rb] = ra
    if rank[ra] == rank[rb]:
        rank[ra] += 1
    return True

union(0, 1)
union(2, 3)
union(1, 3)
union(4, 5)
print("parent:", parent)
print("rank:  ", rank)
props.task: Add union(5, 2) just before the two print lines. Predict which root ends up under which, and whether any rank changes, before you run it.

check.question: Under union by rank, a root with rank 1 is united with a root with rank 2. What happens?
choices: The rank-2 root goes under the rank-1 root
Both ranks increase by one
The rank-1 root goes under the rank-2 root, whose rank becomes 3
The rank-1 root goes under the rank-2 root, and no rank changes
check.explanation: The shorter tree hangs under the taller one, so the taller tree's height does not grow and its rank stays 2. A rank only increases when two roots of equal rank are joined.

sections.title: Union-find at work: components, cycles and valid trees
sections.key: Count groups, catch the edge that closes a cycle, check trees and run Kruskal with union-find; it handles undirected connectivity only, and cannot split groups.
sections.body:
Most union-find interview problems are one of a handful of moves built on find and union:

[[visual]]

Know its limits too, and say why you chose it:

[[visual 2]]

When you explain your plan, state the invariant out loud: each group is a tree, its root names the group, and union only ever links roots.

[[code]]

visual.title: The moves
rows: Start with n; subtract one for every union that merges two roots
Add edges one by one: an edge whose ends already share a root closes a cycle ("redundant connection")
Exactly n - 1 edges and no failed union: then the count fell from n to 1, so it is connected too
Union every equality **first**, then test every inequality. Merging accounts that share an email works the same way
Sort edges by cost and keep each edge whose union succeeds
Sort events by time; stop when the group count reaches 1

items.title: Good fit
points: Undirected connectivity
Edges keep arriving between questions
Cycle edges, components, Kruskal

items.title: Wrong tool
points: Directed cycles: use DFS with colors or Kahn's algorithm
Deleting edges: it cannot split a group
Path lengths: use BFS or Dijkstra
One question on a fixed graph: a DFS is just as fast

sections.pitfall: Using union-find to find cycles in a directed graph. The edges 0 -> 1, 0 -> 2 and 1 -> 2 contain no directed cycle, but union-find reports one at the third edge because it ignores direction.

activity.title: Redundant connection
activity.prompt: Process the cables in order and return the first one whose ends are already connected. Work out why that is also the last removable cable in the input, then try the hidden tests.

check.question: Union-find processes the edges [[1, 2], [3, 4], [2, 3], [1, 4]] on nodes 1 to 4. Which edge is the first whose union fails?
choices: None of them
check.explanation: After [1, 2], [3, 4] and [2, 3] all four nodes share one root, so [1, 4] finds both ends already connected: it closes the cycle 1-2-3-4-1. [2, 3] still merged two separate groups.

sections.title: Prefix sums and difference arrays
sections.key: With prefix array P (P[0] = 0), the sum of nums[left..right] is P[right + 1] - P[left]; a difference array makes each range update O(1) instead.
sections.body:
A dashboard keeps asking for "total sales from day 3 to day 9". Summing the range costs O(n) each time; **prefix sums** answer in O(1) after one O(n) pass.

Build `P` with one extra slot: `P[0] = 0` and `P[i + 1] = P[i] + nums[i]`. The leading zero makes ranges that start at index 0 work without a special case.

[[visual]]

On a grid, `P[r + 1][c + 1]` holds the sum of the block from the top-left corner to (r, c). Build and query it by inclusion and exclusion:

[[visual 2]]

A **difference array** is the reverse tool: many range updates, then one read. Record only the edges, `diff[start] += delta` and `diff[end + 1] -= delta`, and a running sum rebuilds the values.

[[visual 3]]

[[visual 4]]

visual.title: 2D prefix sums
visual.caption: The overlap is added twice, so subtract it once. A query is four reads.

visual.title: Updates (0, 2, +5), (1, 4, +2), (3, 5, -1)
visual.caption: Each value is the running sum of diff up to its index. With +1 at each meeting's start and -1 after its end, the largest running sum is the number of rooms needed.

items.title: Prefix sums
points: Many range-sum queries
O(n) build, O(1) per query

items.title: Difference array
points: Many range updates, read at the end
O(1) per update, O(n) final pass

items.title: Both change at once?
points: Updates and queries interleaved
Fenwick tree or segment tree: O(log n) each

visual.caption: Prefix sums and difference arrays assume the data stops changing while you query it.

sections.code:
P = [0]
for x in [4, 2, 7, 1, 5, 3]:
    P.append(P[-1] + x)         # [0, 4, 6, 13, 14, 19, 22]

def range_sum(left, right):     # inclusive indexes
    return P[right + 1] - P[left]

n = 6
diff = [0] * (n + 1)
for start, end, delta in [(0, 2, 5), (1, 4, 2), (3, 5, -1)]:
    diff[start] += delta        # the change starts here
    diff[end + 1] -= delta      # and stops after end
sections.pitfall: Off-by-one ranges. With the leading 0, the sum of nums[left..right] is P[right + 1] - P[left]. Writing P[right] - P[left] silently drops the last element of every range.

activity.title: Seat bookings with a difference array
activity.prompt: Each booking adds seats to a range of flights. Run it and check flight 2 by hand: it is inside all three bookings, 10 + 20 + 25 = 55. Then do the task.

props.code:
# Each booking reserves seats on a range of flights: (first, last, seats).
flights = 5
bookings = [(1, 2, 10), (2, 3, 20), (2, 5, 25)]

diff = [0] * (flights + 2)          # flights are numbered 1 to 5
for first, last, seats in bookings:
    diff[first] += seats
    diff[last + 1] -= seats

total = 0
for flight in range(1, flights + 1):
    total += diff[flight]
    print("flight", flight, "seats", total)
props.task: Add the booking (4, 5, 5) to the list. Which two diff entries change, and what are the new totals for flights 4 and 5? Predict, then run.
props.expectOutput:
flight 1 seats 10
flight 2 seats 55
flight 3 seats 45
flight 4 seats 30
flight 5 seats 30

check.question: nums = [4, 2, 7, 1, 5, 3] gives P = [0, 4, 6, 13, 14, 19, 22]. What is the sum of nums[2..4] inclusive?
check.explanation: P[5] - P[2] = 19 - 6 = 13, which matches 7 + 1 + 5. P[5] - P[1] = 15 would include index 1, and P[4] - P[2] = 8 would drop index 4.

sections.title: Subarray sum equals k: running totals meet a hash map
sections.key: A subarray ending here sums to k exactly when an earlier running total equals running - k, so a map of totals counts them in O(n), negatives included.
sections.body:
Count the contiguous subarrays of `[2, -1, 1, 2]` that sum to 2. Trying every start and end is O(n^2). A sliding window fails: with negative numbers, adding an element can make the sum smaller, so you cannot tell whether to grow or shrink.

Prefix sums turn the question around. Keep a map from each running total to how many times it has appeared, seeded with `{0: 1}` for the empty prefix so subarrays starting at index 0 count. At each position, add the count of `running - k`.

[[visual]]

**Look up before you record**, or the current total matches itself and counts an empty subarray when k is 0. The same skeleton solves a family of problems, each O(n) time and space:

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

visual.title: Trace with k = 2
visual.caption: After each lookup, the running total is recorded in the map.

visual.title: One skeleton, four problems
rows: Running total to its **first** index, seeded `{0: -1}`; never overwrite, because the earliest start is longest
`running % k` to count: equal remainders differ by a multiple of k. In JavaScript `%` can be negative, so use `((running % k) + k) % k`
Count each 0 as -1, then find the longest subarray with sum 0

sections.code:
def count_sum_k(nums, k):
    seen = {0: 1}                   # running total -> times seen
    running = count = 0
    for x in nums:
        running += x
        count += seen.get(running - k, 0)          # look up first
        seen[running] = seen.get(running, 0) + 1   # then record
    return count

def longest_sum_k(nums, k):
    first = {0: -1}                 # running total -> FIRST index
    running = best = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        running += x
        if running - k in first:
            best = max(best, i - first[running - k])
        first.setdefault(running, i)   # earlier is longer
    return best

print(count_sum_k([2, -1, 1, 2], 2))     # 4
print(longest_sum_k([2, -1, 1, 2], 2))   # 3: [2, -1, 1]
sections.pitfall: Starting the map empty instead of {0: 1}. Subarrays that begin at index 0 are then never counted, so [3] with k = 3 returns 0 instead of 1.

activity.title: Count subarrays that sum to k
activity.prompt: Use a running total and a map of earlier totals, seeded with {0: 1}. Before submitting, run [3, -3, 3, -3] with k = 0 on paper: the answer is 4.

check.question: Why does a sliding window fail for "count subarrays with sum k" when the list contains negative numbers?
choices: Adding an element can lower the sum, so a window that is too big can become valid again
Sliding windows only work on sorted input
Negative numbers cannot be used as hash map keys
The window would need O(n) extra space
check.explanation: A window relies on the sum moving in one direction as it grows. Negative values break that, so shrinking or growing can both be right. Negative numbers are fine map keys, and sorting is not what windows need.

sections.title: Monotonic stacks: next greater, next smaller, biggest rectangle
sections.key: A monotonic stack pops anything that breaks its order, answering next or previous greater and smaller for every index in O(n), because each index is pushed and popped once.
sections.body:
The stacks topic answered "how many days until a warmer day?" with a stack whose values only increase, or only decrease, from bottom to top: a **monotonic stack**. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the scan is O(n) despite the loop inside a loop.

[[visual]]

Store **indexes**, not values, so you can compute distances. Choose `<` or `<=` on purpose for equal values. For a **circular** array, loop over `2n` positions reading `nums[i % n]`, pushing indexes only in the first pass.

The **largest rectangle in a histogram** needs each bar's previous and next smaller bar. One increasing stack finds both: when bar i pops bar j, i is j's next smaller and the new top is its previous smaller. A final height of 0 flushes the stack.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Four questions, four stacks
rows: **Decreasing**. A bigger arrival answers everything it pops
**Increasing**. A smaller arrival answers the bigger values it pops
**Decreasing**. Pop what can never answer again, then read the top
**Increasing**. Pop what can never answer again, then read the top

sections.code:
def previous_smaller(nums):
    """Index of the nearest smaller value to the left, or -1."""
    result, stack = [], []          # stack of indexes, values increasing
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] >= x:
            stack.pop()             # can never be an answer again
        result.append(stack[-1] if stack else -1)
        stack.append(i)
    return result

def largest_rectangle(heights):
    stack, best = [], 0
    for i, h in enumerate(heights + [0]):   # 0 flushes the stack
        while stack and heights[stack[-1]] >= h:
            height = heights[stack.pop()]
            left = stack[-1] + 1 if stack else 0
            best = max(best, height * (i - left))
        stack.append(i)
    return best

print(previous_smaller([3, 1, 4, 1, 5]))    # [-1, -1, 1, -1, 3]
print(largest_rectangle([2, 4, 3, 4, 1]))   # 9
sections.pitfall: Storing values instead of indexes. You lose the positions needed for widths and distances, and equal values become impossible to tell apart.

activity.title: Largest rectangle in a histogram
activity.prompt: Keep an increasing stack of indexes. When a bar pops index j, compute j's rectangle from the new top of the stack. Remember the final 0 that flushes the stack, then test [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].

check.question: With heights [2, 4, 3, 4, 1], which bar pops the 3 off the increasing stack?
choices: The 4 at index 3
The 1 at index 4
The 2 at index 0
The sentinel 0 added at the end
check.explanation: The 4 at index 3 is taller, so it is pushed on top of the 3. The 1 is the first shorter bar to the right of the 3, so it pops it, and the rectangle of height 3 covers indexes 1 to 3 for an area of 9.

sections.tip: Reach for a monotonic stack when a problem asks for the next, previous or nearest larger or smaller value, a span, or how far something can extend.

sections.title: Matrix patterns: spiral, rotate and grid BFS
sections.key: Grids reward care: check bounds, mark cells when you enqueue them, rotate by transposing then reversing rows, and seed BFS with every source when things spread.
sections.body:
Grid problems test care more than cleverness. A small toolkit prevents most bugs:

- Read `rows` and `cols` once and loop over a direction list such as `DIRS = [(1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)]`.
- Check bounds before reading a neighbor: `0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols`.
- Ask before modifying the input; a `seen` set is the safe default.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

**Grid BFS.** A grid is a graph of cells. Counting islands is counting connected components: start a BFS at each unvisited land cell and **mark cells when you enqueue them**.

When something spreads from many places at once (rot, fire), put every source in the queue first: in this **multi-source BFS** each level is one unit of time. To find cells that can reach a border, search backward from the border once.

[[visual 3]]

items.title: Spiral order
points: Four boundaries: walk the top row and move `top` down, the right column and move `right` left, then the bottom row and left column
Check `top <= bottom` before the bottom row and `left <= right` before the left column, or a leftover row or column repeats

items.title: Rotate 90° clockwise
points: Transpose (swap above the diagonal only), then reverse every row
Counterclockwise: transpose, then reverse the row order
Swapping over the whole grid swaps each pair twice and undoes the transpose

items.title: Set matrix zeroes
points: Find all zeros first, write second
Zeros written mid-scan look original and wipe extra rows

steps.label: Count fresh oranges; put every rotten one in the queue
Process the queue one level at a time
Rot each fresh neighbor, lower the fresh count, enqueue it
Add one minute after each level

sections.tip: In Python, prefer an iterative BFS or an explicit stack on big grids. A recursive DFS over a 1,000 by 1,000 grid blows past the default recursion limit of 1,000 calls.
sections.pitfall: Marking a cell visited when you pop it instead of when you push it. The same cell can then sit in the queue many times, which wastes time and double counts in problems that measure steps.

activity.title: Spiral order
activity.prompt: Keep four boundaries and move each one inward after walking its side. Before submitting, trace a single row and a single column: those are where a missing check lists values twice.

check.question: Which pair of in-place steps rotates a square matrix 90 degrees clockwise?
choices: Transpose, then reverse the order of the rows
Reverse each row, then reverse the order of the rows
Transpose, then reverse each row
Transpose twice
check.explanation: Transposing sends (r, c) to (c, r), and reversing each row then sends it to (c, n - 1 - r), which is exactly a clockwise turn. Transpose plus reversing the row order turns it counterclockwise, reversing both ways is a 180 degree turn, and transposing twice changes nothing.

sections.title: Designing a data structure: the LRU cache
sections.key: Design questions combine one structure per need; an O(1) LRU cache is a hash map to find nodes plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency.
sections.body:
Design questions ask for a small data structure with given operations and time limits. They reward a method more than memorized code:

[[visual]]

The **LRU (least recently used) cache** is the classic: `get(key)` and `put(key, value)` both O(1), and when full, a new key evicts the entry unused for longest.

[[visual 2]]

Two **sentinel** nodes, head before the oldest and tail after the newest, mean unlink and append never special-case an empty list. Store the key in each node too: evicting `head.next` must also delete it from the map.

[[visual 3]]

Python's `OrderedDict` packages the pair (`move_to_end`, `popitem(last=False)`), and a JavaScript `Map` keeps insertion order. In an interview, mention the library, then build the list by hand when asked: that is usually the point.

[[visual 4]]

[[code]]

steps.label: Confirm the operations and the time each must take
steps.detail: Ask about capacity, missing keys, what counts as a use

steps.label: List what each operation must find quickly
Pick one structure per need and combine them
steps.detail: Keep every structure in sync on every operation

steps.label: Trace a tiny example, before and after you code

items.title: Hash map
points: Finds a key's node in O(1)
Stores a pointer to each node

items.title: Doubly linked list
points: Keeps entries ordered by recency
Moves a node to the newest end and drops the oldest in O(1)
A node knows both neighbors, so it unlinks in O(1); a singly linked list would walk from the head to find the previous node

Map from key to a time-sorted list, binary searched

sections.deeper:
`functools.lru_cache` applies the same policy to function results: decorate a function and repeated calls with the same arguments return the cached value, evicting the least recently used results once `maxsize` is reached.

A hand-built `get` does three things when the key is present: look up the node in the map, unlink it from its current position, and append it just before the tail sentinel. `put` does the same for an existing key; for a new key it appends a fresh node and, if the cache is now over capacity, unlinks `head.next` and deletes its key from the map.
sections.pitfall: Forgetting that get also counts as a use. If get does not move the key to the newest end, the cache evicts entries that were just read.

activity.title: LRU cache
activity.prompt: Build the hash map plus doubly linked list with head and tail sentinels. Trace the first example by hand before coding: which key does each eviction remove, and why?

check.question: Why does an O(1) LRU cache use a doubly linked list rather than a singly linked one?
choices: Because a singly linked list cannot be stored in a hash map
To keep the keys in sorted order
Because doubly linked lists use less memory
To unlink a node found through the map without walking the list to find its predecessor
check.explanation: Moving or evicting a node means rewiring its predecessor. With a prev pointer that is O(1); a singly linked list needs an O(n) walk from the head. Recency order, not key order, is what the list keeps, and the extra pointer costs memory rather than saving it.

keyTerms.definition: A tree of characters where each node is a prefix; words that share a beginning share a path.
A mark on a trie node meaning a complete word stops there, separating stored words from mere prefixes.
A structure (disjoint set union) that keeps items in groups stored as trees, with find and union in nearly O(1).
Pointing the nodes visited by find directly at their root so later finds are shorter.
Attaching the root of the shorter tree under the taller one so tree heights stay O(log n).
P[i], the sum of the first i values; any range sum is a difference of two prefix sums.
A list of changes between neighbors; a range update edits two entries and a running sum rebuilds the values.
A stack whose values only increase or only decrease, used to find the next or previous larger or smaller element in O(n).
Breadth-first search that starts with every source in the queue, so each level is one unit of distance from the nearest source.
A dummy node at the start or end of a linked list that removes special cases for empty lists and edges.

summary: A trie answers prefix questions in O(L); the end flag separates words from prefixes.
Union-find keeps groups as trees; union by rank and path compression make operations effectively O(1).
Prefix sums give O(1) range sums; difference arrays give O(1) range updates.
A running total plus a map of earlier totals counts subarrays with sum k in O(n).
Monotonic stacks find next and previous larger or smaller values in O(n).
Design questions combine one structure per need: an LRU cache is a hash map plus a doubly linked list.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how a trie finds every word starting with "car" without scanning the whole dictionary, how union-find decides whether two people are in the same group, and why a running total plus a hash map can count the subarrays that add up to k.

questions.question: A trie holds the words "tea", "ten" and "to". How many nodes does it have, counting the root?
questions.explanation: Root, t, te, tea, ten and to: six nodes. "ten" reuses t and e and adds only n, and "to" reuses t and adds o. Shared prefixes are stored once.

questions.question: A trie holds n words. What does search(word) cost for a word of length L?
choices: O(L)
O(n)
O(L log n)
O(n * L)
questions.explanation: search walks one node per letter, so the cost depends only on the word's length. The number of stored words never enters it, which is the point of a trie.

questions.question: Fill the blank so search returns True only for whole inserted words.
choices: len(node.children) == 0
node.children
node is not self.root
node.end
questions.explanation: The end flag records that a word stops at this node. Checking for a leaf fails for "car" when "card" is also stored, because the r node has a child, and node.children only says that longer words exist.

questions.question: After t.insert("card"), t.starts_with("car") returns False. What is wrong?
choices: _walk should follow the letters from last to first
It checks the end flag, which only search needs; a prefix only needs the walk to succeed
The trie must be rebuilt after each insert
starts_with must compare the prefix with every stored word
questions.explanation: "car" is a prefix of "card", so the walk succeeds, but no word ends at r. Dropping the node.end check fixes it. Comparing with every word would work but throws away the O(L) cost.

questions.question: For which tasks is a trie a better fit than a hash set of words? Select all that apply.
choices: Listing every stored word that starts with a given prefix
Checking whether any stored word starts with a prefix
Finding the longest common prefix of all the words
Checking whether one exact word is stored, using as little memory as possible
Counting how many times each word appears in a text
questions.explanation: Prefix questions are what tries are for. For exact membership with low memory, a hash set wins, and counting occurrences is a job for a counting map.

questions.question: To list a prefix's completions in alphabetical order, how should the search below the prefix node work?
choices: Breadth-first, level by level, which gives alphabetical order
Depth-first in the order the letters were inserted
Depth-first visiting children in sorted letter order, adding a word at every end flag
Deepest subtree first, so long words come first
questions.explanation: A depth-first search that visits children in sorted order produces words in dictionary order. Breadth-first lists shorter words first, and insertion order is arbitrary.

questions.question: A trie holds "bad", "bat", "bed" and "bid". How many stored words match the pattern "b.d", where "." is any one letter?
questions.explanation: bad, bed and bid match: b, any letter, d. "bat" ends in t. During the search the dot branches into the a, e and i children, and each branch then needs a d.

questions.question: Each trie node keeps the first three words that pass through it during insertion. Why insert the words in sorted order?
choices: So the first three words to reach a node are its three alphabetically smallest completions
Tries cannot store unsorted words
So that search runs in O(1)
To keep the trie balanced
questions.explanation: Every word below a node passes through it on insertion. In sorted order the earliest three arrivals are the smallest three, so each node's list is exactly the answer for its prefix. Tries need no balancing.

questions.question: Put the steps for finding many words in a letter grid in order.
items: Insert every word into a trie
Start a depth-first search from each grid cell with the trie root
Step to a neighbor only if the current trie node has a child for its letter
Record a word on reaching its end node, then clear that mark
Restore the cell when backtracking out of it
questions.explanation: Building the trie first lets one search follow every word at once. Pruning by trie children stops dead paths, clearing the mark prevents duplicates, and restoring cells lets other paths use them.

questions.question: What simpler approach handles autocomplete for a fixed word list without a trie, and what does it trade?
questions.answer: Sort the words once, binary search for the first word that is at least the prefix, and read forward while words still start with it. It uses far less memory than a trie, at the cost of an O(L log n) search per query instead of an O(L) walk.
questions.explanation: Offering this alternative shows you weigh memory against speed instead of reaching for the fanciest structure.

questions.question: parent = [0, 0, 1, 2, 4]. What does find(3) return?
questions.explanation: 3 points to 2, 2 points to 1, 1 points to 0, and 0 points to itself, so 0 is the root that names 3's group. Node 4 is a separate group of one.

questions.question: parent = [0, 0, 1, 2, 4]. After one call to find(3) with recursive path compression, what is parent?
questions.explanation: Every node on the path from 3 to the root (3, 2 and 1) is pointed straight at 0 as the recursion unwinds. Node 4 was not on the path, so it is untouched.

questions.question: After union(0, 1) and then union(2, 1), find(0) and find(1) differ, although 0 and 1 were joined. What is the bug?
choices: It should set parent[a] = b instead
It links the items, not their roots; it should set parent[find(b)] = find(a)
It must reset rank[b] to 0
parent must be a dict, not a list
questions.explanation: union(2, 1) repoints 1 at 2, pulling 1 out of the group it shared with 0. Linking the roots merges the whole groups and never detaches anyone. Swapping the direction has the same flaw.

questions.question: Match each union-find term with its meaning.

pairs.right: A node whose parent is itself; it names the group
Points the nodes on a find path straight at the root
Hangs the shorter tree under the taller one
An upper bound on the height of a root's tree
Inverse Ackermann function, at most 4 in practice

questions.explanation: Together, union by rank and path compression make each operation O(α(n)) amortized, which you can treat as constant.

questions.question: With neither union by rank nor path compression, what is the worst-case cost of one find on n items?
choices: O(log n)
O(n)
O(α(n))
questions.explanation: Unions such as union(1, 0), union(2, 1), union(3, 2) can build a chain, and find from the bottom walks all of it. Union by rank alone caps the height at O(log n); both tricks together give O(α(n)).

questions.question: With the lesson's DSU (union by rank) on four items, you run union(0, 1), union(2, 3), then union(1, 3). What is the rank of the final root?
questions.explanation: The first two unions create roots 0 and 2, each with rank 1. union(1, 3) joins those two roots; their ranks are equal, so 2 goes under 0 and 0's rank rises to 2.

questions.question: Five nodes start as five groups. Union-find processes the edges (0, 1), (1, 2), (3, 4) and (0, 2). How many groups remain?
questions.explanation: The first three edges each merge two groups: 5 to 4 to 3 to 2. (0, 2) finds both ends in the same group, so it merges nothing and closes a cycle. The groups are {0, 1, 2} and {3, 4}.

questions.question: n = 5 nodes and edges = [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 3]]. Is it a valid tree?
choices: No: a tree on 5 nodes needs 4 edges, and node 4 is cut off
Yes: no edge closes a cycle
Yes: every union merged two groups
No: the edges form a cycle
questions.explanation: No cycle is not enough. Three successful unions take five groups down to two, so the graph is disconnected. That is why the check requires exactly n - 1 edges as well as no failed union.

questions.question: Which problems are a good fit for union-find? Select all that apply.
choices: Counting connected components while edges keep arriving
Finding the edge that closes a cycle in an undirected graph
Building a minimum spanning tree with Kruskal's algorithm
Finding the shortest path in a weighted graph
Detecting a cycle in a directed dependency graph
questions.explanation: Union-find tracks undirected connectivity. Shortest paths need BFS or Dijkstra, and directed cycles need DFS with colors or Kahn's algorithm, because union-find ignores edge direction.

questions.question: For ["a!=c", "a==b", "b==c"] this returns True, but the equations contradict each other. What is the fix?
choices: Compare with find(a) != find(b) in the elif instead
Sort the equations alphabetically first
Use union by rank so that find gives the right root
Union every == equation in a first pass, then check every != in a second pass
questions.explanation: "a!=c" is checked while a and c are still in different groups, and only later do a==b and b==c merge them. Checking inequalities after all merges sees the final groups. Sorting by text does not reliably put equalities first.

questions.question: Why does Kruskal's algorithm skip an edge whose two ends already have the same root?
questions.answer: Its ends are already connected by cheaper edges chosen earlier, so the edge would only close a cycle and add cost without connecting anything new.
questions.explanation: Sorting by cost plus "take it only if it joins two groups" is the whole algorithm, and union-find makes the check nearly O(1).

questions.question: P = [0, 3, 5, 10, 11, 17] is the prefix array of some list nums, with P[0] = 0. What is the sum of nums[1..3] inclusive?
questions.explanation: P[4] - P[1] = 11 - 3 = 8. Reading nums back from P gives [3, 2, 5, 1, 6], and 2 + 5 + 1 = 8.

questions.question: Fill the blank so range_sum returns nums[left] + ... + nums[right], given P with a leading 0.
questions.code:
def range_sum(left, right):
    return P[_____] - P[left]
choices: right
right + 1
right - 1
left + 1
questions.explanation: P[i] is the sum of the first i values, so the sum through index right is P[right + 1]. P[right] stops one element short.

questions.question: n = 5 and the list starts as zeros. With a difference array you apply [1, 3, +4] and [0, 1, -1] (start, end inclusive, delta). What is the final list?
questions.explanation: diff becomes [-1, 4, 1, 0, -4, 0], and its running sum is [-1, 3, 4, 4, 0]. Index 1 gets both updates (4 - 1 = 3). [-1, 4, 1, 0, -4] is the raw diff before the running sum.

questions.question: For the grid [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]], what is the sum of the rectangle from cell (1, 1) to cell (2, 2)?
Thousands of point updates and range-sum queries arrive interleaved. Which structure fits best?
choices: A Fenwick tree or segment tree, O(log n) for both
A prefix sum array rebuilt after every update
A difference array
A hash map from index to value
questions.explanation: Prefix sums make queries O(1) but every update O(n) to rebuild. A difference array is built for range updates read at the end. Fenwick and segment trees keep both operations at O(log n).

questions.question: For nums = [5], range_sum(0, 0) returns 0 instead of 5. What is the fix?
choices: Start P as an empty list instead of [0]
Return P[right] - P[left - 1]
Start the loop at the second element
Return P[right + 1] - P[left]; with the leading 0, P[right] stops one element short
questions.explanation: P = [0, 5], and the sum of the first right + 1 values is P[right + 1] = 5. P[left - 1] would read P[-1] when left is 0, which in Python is the last entry.

questions.question: How many contiguous subarrays of [1, -1, 1, -1] sum to 0?
questions.explanation: [1, -1] twice, [-1, 1] once, and the whole list. In the running-total method, the totals 1, 0, 1, 0 match earlier totals 0, 1, 1 and 2 times, after seeding the map with {0: 1}.

questions.question: Why is the map of running totals seeded with {0: 1}?
choices: It prevents a KeyError when k is 0
It represents the empty prefix, so subarrays that start at index 0 are counted
It counts the empty subarray as a valid answer
It keeps the map from ever being empty
questions.explanation: A subarray starting at index 0 sums to running - 0, so it needs an earlier total of 0: the empty prefix. The empty subarray is never counted because the lookup happens before the current total is recorded.

questions.question: Fill the blank so the function returns the length of the longest subarray that sums to k.
choices: first[running] = i
first[running - k] = i
first.setdefault(running, i)
first.pop(running, None)
questions.explanation: setdefault records a total only the first time it appears, and the earliest start gives the longest subarray. first[running] = i would overwrite it with later indexes and find shorter subarrays.

questions.question: In JavaScript, -7 % 5 is -2. Why does that matter when counting subarrays whose sum is divisible by 5?
choices: Remainders -2 and 3 mean the same thing mod 5 but become different map keys, so matching prefixes are missed
A JavaScript Map cannot use negative keys
The % operator is slower on negative numbers
It does not matter, because -2 and 3 are different remainders
questions.explanation: Two prefixes whose difference is a multiple of 5 must share a key. Normalizing with ((running % k) + k) % k maps -2 to 3. Python's % already returns a non-negative result for a positive k.

questions.question: What is the next greater element (to the right, no wrapping, -1 if none) for each value of [2, 7, 3, 5, 4, 6, 1]?
questions.explanation: 3 waits for 5, and both 5 and 4 wait for 6. Nothing to the right of 7 or 6 is larger, and 1 is last. [7, -1, 5, 6, 6, 7, 2] is the circular answer, where 6 and 1 wrap around.

questions.question: When you compute the next smaller element to the right, in what order are the values on the stack from bottom to top?
choices: Decreasing
Increasing
Any order, because only the indexes matter
All equal
questions.explanation: A smaller arrival pops every larger value above it, so whatever remains under each new push is smaller or equal: the stack increases from bottom to top. Next greater uses the opposite order.

questions.question: What is the area of the largest rectangle in the histogram [3, 1, 3, 2, 2]?
questions.explanation: Height 2 across the last three bars (3, 2, 2) gives 6. Height 1 across all five bars gives only 5, and a single bar of height 3 gives 3.

questions.question: How do you find the next greater element in a circular array with a monotonic stack?
questions.answer: Loop i from 0 to 2n - 1 and read nums[i % n], so values near the end can find answers that wrap around to the start. Push indexes only in the first pass (i < n), but keep popping in both passes.
questions.explanation: The second pass only answers elements still waiting; pushing again would give them a second, wrong answer.

questions.question: Why is a monotonic stack scan O(n) even though it has a while loop inside a for loop?
choices: The while loop runs at most once per iteration
The stack never holds more than two items
Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the while loop runs at most n times in total
Python merges the nested loops into one
questions.explanation: Count work across the whole scan, not per iteration: one iteration may pop many items, but every pop removes an index that can never return. The total is at most n pushes and n pops.

questions.question: A spiral order on the 3 x 4 grid of 1 to 12 returns [1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 12, 11, 10, 9, 5, 6, 7, 6]. Which check is missing?
choices: top <= bottom before walking the bottom row
left <= right before walking the top row
rows == cols at the start
A visited set for the top row
questions.explanation: On the second lap only the row 6, 7 is left. After it is walked, top passes bottom, so there is no bottom row, but without the check the code walks it anyway and lists 6 again.

questions.question: Put the steps of the multi-source BFS for rotting oranges in order.
items: Count the fresh oranges and put every rotten one in the queue
Process the queue one level at a time
Rot each fresh neighbor, lower the fresh count and enqueue it
Add one minute after each level
Return the minutes if no fresh orange remains, otherwise -1
questions.explanation: Starting with every source in the queue makes level k the set of oranges that rot at minute k. The fresh count tells you at the end whether any orange was unreachable.

questions.question: This island BFS gives the right count but is very slow on a large grid that is all land. Why?
choices: popleft is O(n) on a deque
The direction list should include diagonals
seen should be a list, not a set
Cells are marked when popped, so one cell can be queued many times before it is processed
questions.explanation: Until a cell is popped, every neighbor that looks at it sees it as unvisited and enqueues it again. Adding to seen at the moment of appending makes each cell enter the queue once. deque.popleft is O(1).

questions.question: You transpose [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and then reverse each row. What is the result?
questions.explanation: The transpose is [[1, 3], [2, 4]]; reversing each row gives [[3, 1], [4, 2]], the matrix turned 90 degrees clockwise. [[4, 3], [2, 1]] is a 180 degree turn.

questions.question: In the hand-built LRU cache, what must get(key) do when the key is present? Select all that apply.
choices: Look up the key's node in the map
Unlink the node from its current position
Append the node just before the tail sentinel
Remove the node at head.next
Create a new node for the key
questions.explanation: A successful get is a use, so the node moves to the newest end. Evicting head.next only happens in put when a new key arrives and the cache is full, and get never creates nodes.

questions.question: An LRU cache has capacity 2. You run put(1, 1), put(2, 2), get(1), put(3, 3), then get(2). What does the final get(2) return?
questions.explanation: get(1) makes key 2 the least recently used, so put(3, 3) evicts key 2. Without the get, key 1 would have been evicted instead.

questions.question: Match each design problem with the structures that meet its time limits.

pairs.right: Hash map plus doubly linked list
Array plus a map from value to index
Max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper
Map from key to a time-sorted list, binary searched

questions.explanation: Each design pairs one structure per need: fast lookup by key, fast order or extreme value, or fast random access, kept in sync on every operation.

questions.question: Why does each node in the hand-built LRU list store its key as well as its value?
choices: So the list can be kept sorted by key
Because the map stores only values
So that evicting head.next can also delete its entry from the map
To detect cycles in the list
questions.explanation: Eviction starts from the list, not the map. The evicted node has to tell you which map entry to delete, and without its key you would have to search the map.

questions.question: What steps would you follow to answer a "design a data structure" interview question?
questions.answer: Confirm the operations and the time each must take, list what each operation needs to find quickly, choose one structure per need and combine them, keep them in sync on every operation, then trace a small example.
questions.explanation: Saying these steps out loud shows structured thinking even before the code works, which is much of what the interviewer is assessing.
